title: Protein structure and function; How enzymes work
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EZ01a#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM08a#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM08a#t3 term and clue written for the game; BM08b#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM08a#N.4a, EZ01a#N.2a, BM08a#N.10a, EZ01a#N.10a, BM08a#N.13, EZ01a#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Active site
items.clue: Small pocket or groove on an enzyme where the substrate binds.

items.label: Primary structure
items.clue: The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, held by peptide bonds

items.label: Tertiary structure
items.clue: Overall 3D shape of one folded chain, held by bonds between R groups

items.label: Haemoglobin
items.clue: Soluble protein of two α and two β polypeptides that carries up to four O₂

questions.stem: What stabilises the alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets of a protein's secondary structure?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds at regular positions between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone.
Ionic bonds between charged amine and carboxyl groups spaced regularly along the backbone.
Disulfide bonds between cysteines spaced at regular intervals along the polypeptide.
Hydrogen bonds forming the peptide links between the amine and carboxyl groups of neighbours.

questions.explanation: Helices and sheets are held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one peptide bond and the N–H of another, at regular positions along the backbone.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how an enzyme acts as a catalyst in a cell?

options.text: It is converted into product along with the substrate, so the cell must keep making it.
It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all in its absence in the cell.
It transfers energy to the substrate so that the reaction is driven forward faster.
It increases the rate of a reaction that could occur without it, and is released unchanged.

questions.explanation: Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that would otherwise occur far too slowly at cell temperature, and each molecule catalyses the reaction repeatedly.

questions.stem: When egg white is heated, its soluble proteins turn into a white solid. What has happened to the protein molecules?

options.text: Heat has broken the bonds holding their folded shape, so they have unfolded.
Heat has broken the peptide bonds, so the polypeptides have been split into amino acids.
Heat has killed the proteins, so they are no longer able to carry out their functions.
Heat has changed their shape temporarily, and they will refold as soon as the egg white cools.

questions.explanation: This is denaturation. Extra vibration breaks the bonds that hold the 3D shape; the unfolded chains tangle together, so the egg white becomes an insoluble solid.

questions.stem: Lipase catalyses the hydrolysis of triglycerides but has no effect on starch. What is the reason?

options.text: Starch molecules are too large to enter the active site, but any molecule smaller than starch could.
The active site of lipase is complementary in shape and chemical properties to a triglyceride only.
Starch requires more energy to break down than lipase is able to supply to the reaction.
Lipase seeks out triglyceride molecules in the fluid and ignores starch molecules it meets.

questions.explanation: Specificity arises from the structure of the active site: its shape and chemical properties match one substrate, so starch cannot bind in a way that allows catalysis.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces one amino acid in an enzyme at a position on the surface far from the active site in the folded protein. The enzyme loses most of its activity. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The result must be an error, because only the amino acids of the active site itself can affect catalysis
The change disturbs interactions that hold the enzyme's overall shape, altering the active site
The loss of activity shows the enzyme has been denatured, so its chain has broken up into free amino acids
The changed amino acid supplies less energy to the reaction, so the substrate cannot react

questions.stem: In a hypothetical bacterium, enzyme E catalyses the conversion of compound A to compound B. The conversion of A to B releases energy. A mutation stops the bacterium from making enzyme E. No other enzyme in the bacterium acts on compound A. Which prediction about compound B in the mutant bacterium is best supported?

options.text: B no longer forms at all, as A cannot change into B without enzyme E.
B forms at the normal rate, as the bacterium makes a new enzyme because it needs B.
B forms at the normal rate, as ATP supplies the energy that enzyme E used to supply.
B still forms, but far more slowly, as the reaction is no longer catalysed.
